title: Tree Data Structure
html:
You already know the traversals and height(). This topic is the problem toolkit for binary trees: level-by-level BFS, horizontal distances, the return height, record the answer on the side pattern, two-stack tricks and (de)serialisation — the handful of techniques behind almost every tree interview question.

Binary tree — a hierarchical structure in which every node has at most two children, left and right. Unlike a BST there is no ordering rule, so every problem here must be solved by visiting nodes, not by comparing keys.

Conventions used in these notes

TermMeaning hereSample tree
Heightnumber of nodes on the longest root-to-leaf path; an empty tree has height 04 (10 → 30 → 70 → 80)
Levelroot is level 0, its children level 1, …4 levels (0–3)
Diameternumber of nodes on the longest path between any two nodes6 (40 20 10 30 70 80)
Horizontal distance (hd)root 0; a left child is hd − 1, a right child hd + 140 is at −2, 90 at +3
Balancedfor every node, |height(left) − height(right)| ≤ 1yes
Completeall levels full except possibly the last, which is filled left to rightno (gap under 40/50/60)
Key point

Height is counted in nodes here, as in the original notes (a single node has height 1). Some books count edges — then every formula shifts by one. State your convention in an interview before writing code.

Node class and the sample tree

Every program in this topic starts with the same Node class and a sample() builder that constructs the tree above by nesting constructor calls. Here it is with three warm-ups you already know: inorder, height and node count.

Key point

JavaScript's console.log always ends the line, so the programs use process.stdout.write when a value must be followed by a space instead of a newline — exactly what print(x, end=" ") does in Python.

The technique toolbox

Almost every problem below is one of five patterns. Recognise the pattern and the code writes itself.

Level-by-level BFS

Queue; take len(queue) nodes per round. Gives level order, width, zigzag, bottom view.

Return height, record on the side

A post-order recursion returns one value (height) while a shared variable collects the answer: balanced, diameter, burn time.

Horizontal distance map

Carry hd with each node; group by it in an ordered map: vertical traversal, top/bottom view.

Preorder + inorder

Preorder gives the root, inorder splits left from right: tree construction, serialisation.

Explicit stack

Simulate the recursion yourself: iterative inorder/preorder, two-stack spiral.

Structural shortcuts

Exploit shape: a perfect subtree has 2^h − 1 nodes, so a complete tree is counted in O(log² n).

Level order traversal line by line

Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 10 | 20 30 | 40 50 60 70 | 80 90 (| = new line)

Plain BFS prints all keys on one line. To start a new line after every level you need to know where a level ends. There are two classic ways.

Idea

Method 1 — a marker. Push a None sentinel after the root. Whenever the sentinel comes out of the queue the current level is finished: print a newline and push the sentinel again so it sits behind the next level. Stop when the sentinel is the only thing left.

Time O(n)Space O(w) — w = maximum width
Pitfall

Looping while q instead of while len(q) > 1 never terminates: the marker keeps re-adding itself to an otherwise empty queue. In Java, ArrayDeque throws on add(null) — use LinkedList for this method, or the count method below which needs no marker.

Idea

Method 2 — count the level. At the start of each round len(queue) is exactly the number of nodes on the current level. Pop that many, printing them and enqueuing their children, then print a newline. No sentinel, no special cases — this is the version to remember, and the backbone of width, zigzag and bottom-view problems.

Time O(n)Space O(w)
Pitfall

Read len(q) once, before the inner loop. Writing for _ in range(len(q)) is safe in Python because the range is evaluated once, but while i < q.size() in C++/Java re-reads a size that grows as children are added and merges levels.

Check for balanced binary tree

Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: Yes
Input: the sample tree with 100 added under 80
Output: No

Idea

Naive: for every node compute the heights of both subtrees and compare, then recurse into the children. Correct, but height() is itself O(n), and it is called again for every node — O(n · h), which is O(n²) on a skewed tree.

Time O(n · h) — O(n²) when skewedSpace O(h) recursion
Idea

Efficient — the −1 trick. Let one post-order function return the height of a subtree, but return −1 as soon as any subtree is unbalanced. A parent that receives −1 from a child passes it straight up without recursing further. Each node is visited once, so the whole check is O(n).

Time O(n)Space O(h)
Pattern

The same shape — a post-order function that returns one quantity and smuggles a second one out — solves diameter, burn time and many more. Learn it once.

Vertical traversal

Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 40 | 20 | 10 50 60 | 30 80 | 70 | 90 (| = new line, one line per column)

Idea

Carry the horizontal distance with every node in a level-order traversal and group keys by it in an ordered map. BFS order guarantees that inside one column the upper node comes before the lower one, and that at the same level the left one comes first — exactly the order a vertical traversal wants. Sorting the keys of the map (or using an ordered map) prints the columns from left to right.

Time O(n log n) — sorting / ordered map over the columnsSpace O(n)
Pitfall

Use BFS, not a preorder DFS, to fill the map. With DFS the node 50 (hd 0, level 2) would be recorded before 60 (hd 0, level 2) — fine — but 80 (hd 1, level 3) would come before 30 (hd 1, level 1), which is wrong: within a column the order must be top to bottom.

Bottom view of a binary tree

Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 40 20 60 80 70 90
Input: the original notes' tree 10(20(30, 40), 50(60, 70))
Output: 30 20 60 50 70

Idea

The bottom view shows, for every column (hd), the lowest node — and when two nodes share both the column and the level, the one further to the right (the one BFS visits later). So run the same hd-tagged BFS and simply let every node overwrite its column's entry: the last write per column is the bottom view. Keeping the first write per column instead gives the top view for free.

Time O(n log n)Space O(n)
Key point

In the original notes' tree, 40 (right child of 20) and 60 (left child of 50) both sit at hd 0 on the same level. BFS visits 40 first and 60 second, so 60 overwrites and wins — that is the convention: ties go to the node further right. Had you used a DFS the winner would depend on traversal order, which is why the queue matters here.

Maximum width of a binary tree

Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 4 (level 2 holds 40 50 60 70)
Input: the original notes' tree 10(20(40(80)), 30(50, 60))
Output: 3

Idea

Width is the number of nodes on a level, and the level-by-level BFS already knows that number: it is len(queue) at the start of each round. Keep the maximum over all rounds — no printing needed.

Time O(n)Space O(w)
Variant

This counts present nodes per level. LeetCode's Maximum Width of Binary Tree counts the span between the leftmost and rightmost node including gaps — for that, carry an index i with each node (2i and 2i + 1 for its children) and take last − first + 1 per level.

Convert a binary tree to a doubly linked list

Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 40 <-> 20 <-> 50 <-> 10 <-> 60 <-> 30 <-> 80 <-> 70 <-> 90
Input: the original notes' tree 10(5, 20(30, 35))
Output: 5 <-> 10 <-> 30 <-> 20 <-> 35

Idea

The list must be in inorder, and the node's own left / right pointers become prev / next — no new nodes. Do an inorder traversal and keep a shared prev, the node visited just before the current one: link prev.right = node, node.left = prev, then advance prev. The first node ever visited (when prev is still None) is the head.

Time O(n)Space O(h) recursion — no extra nodes
Pitfall

Recurse into node.left before touching node.left — the recursion needs the original pointer. Setting node.left = prev first and then calling to_dll(node.left) walks back into the list and loops forever. The same applies to prev: it must be a variable shared across all calls (global / static / closure), not a parameter, or a deeper call's update is lost.

Construct a binary tree from inorder and preorder

Example

Input: pre = [10 20 40 50 30 60 70 80 90], in = [40 20 50 10 60 30 80 70 90]
Output: the sample tree (printed level by level)
Input: pre = [10 20 30], in = [20 10 30]
Output: 10 | 20 30

Idea

Preorder tells you the root, inorder tells you the split. The first preorder key is the root. Find it in the inorder sequence: everything to its left is the left subtree, everything to its right is the right subtree. Recurse on the two halves, consuming preorder keys from a shared index — the left subtree is built first, so it takes the next keys, exactly as preorder lays them out.

The straightforward version searches the inorder slice linearly for the root — O(n) per node, O(n²) in total on a skewed tree:

Idea

Efficient: store the inorder position of every key in a hash map once (O(n)); then each root is located in O(1) and the whole tree is built in O(n). This is the version to remember.

Time O(n)Space O(n) for the map + O(h) recursion
Pitfall

Build the left subtree before the right one — the shared preorder index only works in that order. And the method assumes distinct keys: with duplicates the inorder position is ambiguous and no inorder + preorder pair identifies a unique tree. (Inorder + postorder works the same way, reading postorder from the back; preorder + postorder alone is not enough.)

Corrected

The original notes' 'efficient' version used a stack and stack[-1].key in io[:mp[value]], which re-scans a slice of the inorder list for every node — O(n²) again. The hash-map recursion above is the genuinely linear version.

Spiral (zigzag) level order traversal

Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 10 30 20 40 50 60 70 90 80
Input: the original notes' tree 10(5, 20(30, 35))
Output: 10 20 5 30 35

Even levels (0, 2, …) are printed left to right, odd levels right to left — so level 1 of the sample prints 30 20 and level 3 prints 90 80.

Idea

Method 1 — level order + a stack. Run the count-based level-by-level BFS. On a normal level print each node as it is dequeued; on a reversed level push the keys onto a stack instead and pop them all once the level is done — popping reverses the order. Toggle the flag after every level.

Time O(n)Space O(w)
Idea

Method 2 — two stacks. Let s1 hold the current left-to-right level and s2 the next one. Pop everything from s1, printing and pushing each node's children left then right into s2; because a stack reverses, s2 now pops right to left. Then pop everything from s2, pushing children right then left into s1, which reverses them back. Each stack hands the other exactly one level, already in the required order.

1
Start
Push the root onto s1.
2
While either stack is non-empty
Drain s1 (prints left → right): for each popped node push left, then right onto s2.
3
Then drain s2
(prints right → left): for each popped node push right, then left onto s1.
Time O(n)Space O(w)
Pitfall

The two inner loops push children in opposite orders (left, right into s2 but right, left into s1). Swap one of them and every other level comes out in the wrong direction — trace the sample by hand once and the asymmetry becomes obvious.

Diameter of a binary tree

Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 6 (40 → 20 → 10 → 30 → 70 → 80, counted in nodes)

Idea

For every node, the longest path through it has 1 + height(left) + height(right) nodes. The diameter is the maximum of this value over all nodes. Naive: compute it at every node with a fresh height() call — O(n · h):

Idea

Efficient — return height, record the diameter on the side. The post-order function returns the height of its subtree (what the parent needs) and, before returning, updates a shared best with 1 + lh + rh (what the problem wants). Every node is visited once. The notes' intermediate version — a first pass that stores every height in a hash map, then a second pass — is also O(n), but the single-pass version below needs no map.

Time O(n)Space O(h)
Pitfall

Do not return the diameter from the recursion — the parent needs the height. Returning max(lh, rh) + 1 while storing 1 + lh + rh elsewhere is the whole trick. (If the question counts edges, the answer is lh + rh with heights in edges — one less than here: 5 for the sample.)

Lowest common ancestor (LCA)

Example

Input: the sample tree, (40, 50)
Output: 20
Input: (80, 30)
Output: 30
Input: (50, 90)
Output: 10
Input: (80, 90)
Output: 70

Lowest common ancestor of `a` and `b` — the deepest node that has both a and b in its subtree. A node counts as its own ancestor, so LCA(80, 30) = 30.

Idea

Method 1 — two root-to-node paths. Record the path from the root to a and to b (a DFS that appends on the way down and pops on backtracking). Both paths start at the root; walk them in parallel while they agree — the last common node is the LCA. Two traversals and two O(h) paths; it also reports when a key is missing.

Time O(n)Space O(h) for the two paths
Idea

Method 2 — one traversal. Ask each node what does your subtree contain? A node returns itself if its key is a or b; otherwise it asks both children. If both sides return something, the two keys are on different sides and this node is the LCA. If only one side does, pass that result up — it is either the LCA found deeper or the single key seen so far. Four cases, one post-order pass.

Case at node nReturn
n is a or bn (no need to look below: if the other key is beneath, n is still the LCA)
left returns a node and right returns a noden — the keys are on different sides
only one side returns a nodethat node (both keys are below it, or only one was found)
neither side returns a nodeNone
Time O(n)Space O(h)
Pitfall

Method 2 assumes both keys exist. Ask for LCA(40, 999) and it happily returns 40 — the single key it found — because case 1 stops looking. Method 1 reports the missing key correctly. If keys may be absent, either verify existence first or have the recursion also return how many of the two keys it saw.

Burn a binary tree from a leaf

Example

Input: the sample tree, fire starts at leaf 50
Output: 5
Input: fire starts at leaf 60
Output: 4
Input: the original notes' tree 10(20(40, 50), 30(60)), leaf 50
Output: 4

Idea

The farthest node from the leaf is reached by going up to some ancestor and then down into that ancestor's other subtree. So for every ancestor n of the leaf, the candidate answer is dist(leaf, n) + height(other child of n). One post-order pass computes both: the function returns the height of a subtree (like before) and reports the leaf's distance through an out-parameter dist (−1 when the leaf is not below). At a node where dist came back from one side, update the answer with the other side's height.

Time O(n)Space O(h)
Pitfall

The function returns 1 at the leaf and uses dist + height — this only adds up when the fire really starts at a leaf. Starting at an internal node also needs max(lh, rh) of that node's own subtree as a candidate, and the height returned there must be the real height, not 1. Interviewers love asking for that generalisation (minimum time to burn from any node); the BFS-on-parent-pointers approach handles it directly.

Count nodes in a complete binary tree

Example

Input: complete tree 10(20(40(80, 90), 50(100)), 30(60, 70))
Output: 10
Input: perfect tree 10(20(40, 50), 30(60, 70))
Output: 7

Idea

1 + count(left) + count(right) is O(n) and works for any tree. A complete tree has structure to exploit: walk down the leftmost and the rightmost path of a subtree. If the two heights are equal the subtree is perfect and has exactly 2^h − 1 nodes — no need to visit them. Otherwise recurse into both children, but at least one of them is perfect and answers immediately, so only one branch keeps recursing. O(log n) levels × O(log n) to measure the two heights = O(log² n).

Time O(log² n)Space O(log n)
Pitfall

The shortcut is only valid for a complete tree. On an arbitrary tree lh == rh does not imply a perfect subtree (a node with a left-only chain of 2 and a right-only chain of 2 has equal heights but 5 nodes, not 7) — use the plain O(n) count there. This is also why heaps, which are complete trees, can live in arrays.

Serialize and deserialize a binary tree

Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 10 20 40 -1 -1 50 -1 -1 30 60 -1 -1 70 80 -1 -1 90 -1 -1 (preorder, −1 = empty)
Input: the original notes' tree 10(20, 30)
Output: 10 20 -1 -1 30 -1 -1

Serialization — turning a tree into a flat sequence (string or array) that can be stored or sent, such that deserialization rebuilds exactly the same tree. A single traversal order is not enough on its own — 10 20 could be a left child or a right child.

Idea

Approach A — inorder + separator + preorder. Two traversals identify a tree with distinct keys (see Construct from inorder and preorder). Store the inorder, a separator such as −1, then the preorder, and rebuild with the hash-map construction. It works, but needs distinct keys and twice the space:

Idea

Approach B — preorder with explicit empties (the one to remember). A preorder traversal becomes unambiguous as soon as every missing child is written down too: emit the key, recurse left, recurse right, and emit −1 for None. Deserialization reads the sequence in the same order with a shared index: read a value; if it is −1 return None, otherwise create the node and build its left then right child from the following values. Duplicates are fine, and the output is 2n + 1 values.

Time O(n)Space O(n) — 2n + 1 values
Pitfall

The read index must be shared across the recursive calls (a global, a reference, or a one-element list) — passing an int by value makes every call re-read the same position. And reset it to 0 before deserializing a second sequence. If −1 can be a real key, pick a different marker (a string such as # or N in a text format).

Iterative inorder traversal

Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 40 20 50 10 60 30 80 70 90
Input: the original notes' tree 10(20(40, 50), 30)
Output: 40 20 10 30

Idea

Recursion keeps the pending nodes on the call stack; do it yourself with an explicit stack. From the current node, push every node on the way down the left spine. Then pop: the popped node is the next one in inorder (its left side is finished), print it, and move to its right child — and push that child's left spine in the same way. Stop when both the stack and the current pointer are empty.

1
Go left
While curr is not empty: push curr, curr = curr.left.
2
Visit
Pop the stack into curr and print it — everything to its left has been printed.
3
Go right
curr = curr.right, then repeat from step 1. Finished when the stack is empty and curr is empty.
Time O(n)Space O(h) stack
Key point

The loop condition is stack or curr, not just stack: after popping the root (10) the stack may be empty while curr still points at the unvisited right subtree. The original notes avoided this by pre-pushing the left spine before the loop and re-pushing inside it — equivalent, but with the spine-push code written twice.

Iterative preorder traversal

Example

Input: the sample tree
Output: 10 20 40 50 30 60 70 80 90
Input: the original notes' tree 10(20(40, 50), 30(60))
Output: 10 20 40 50 30 60

Idea

Version 1 — push right, then left. Preorder visits a node before its children, so a node can be printed the moment it is popped. Push the root; then repeatedly pop, print, and push the right child first and the left child second — the stack is LIFO, so the left child comes out next, exactly as preorder requires.

Time O(n)Space O(n) worst case — the stack can hold up to half the nodes
Idea

Version 2 — push only right children (space-optimised). Left children never need the stack: walk down the left spine printing each node as you go, and push only the right children you pass. When the spine ends, pop the most recent right child and continue from it. The stack now holds at most one node per level — O(h) instead of O(n).

Time O(n)Space O(h) stack
TraversalIterative trickStack holds
Inorderpush the left spine, pop–print, go rightO(h)
Preorder v1pop–print, push right then leftup to O(n)
Preorder v2print on the way down the left spine, push right children onlyO(h)
Postorderpreorder with children swapped (root, right, left), then reverse the output — or two stacksO(n)
Level ordera queue instead of a stackO(w)
Pitfall

Version 1 pushes the right child before the left. Push them the other way round and you get 10 30 70 90 80 60 20 50 40 — a mirrored preorder. The rule of thumb for every stack-based traversal: push in the reverse of the order you want to see.

Interview Q&A

Height, depth, level, diameter — what is the difference, and does it count nodes or edges?

Depth of a node is its distance from the root; level is depth (root = level 0). Height of a node is the longest downward path to a leaf; height of the tree is the root's height. Diameter is the longest path between any two nodes. Each may be counted in nodes or edges — the two conventions differ by one (a single node has height 1 in nodes, 0 in edges). These notes count nodes, like the original; say which you use before you code, and remember that the edge-diameter is lh + rh while the node-diameter is 1 + lh + rh.

Why does the 'return height, record the answer on the side' pattern keep showing up?

Because many tree quantities (balanced, diameter, burn time, maximum path sum) are defined per node as a combination of its two subtree heights, yet a parent only needs the height back. A single post-order pass returns the height to the parent and updates a shared answer variable as a side effect — O(n) instead of the O(n · h) you get from calling height() afresh at every node. Balanced-check uses −1 as a poison value so the recursion short-circuits.

Which traversals uniquely determine a binary tree?

Inorder together with preorder (or postorder) and distinct keys: the (pre/post)order supplies the root, the inorder splits left from right. Preorder + postorder alone do not (a root with a single child is ambiguous). Any single order determines a tree only if empties are recorded too — which is exactly the preorder-with-−1 serialization. For a BST preorder alone suffices, since inorder is implied by sorting.

How do the bottom view, top view and vertical traversal differ in code?

All three run the same BFS with a horizontal distance per node and a map keyed by hd. Vertical traversal appends every key to its column; top view keeps the first key per column (putIfAbsent); bottom view keeps the last (overwrite on every visit). BFS, not DFS, is what guarantees the top-to-bottom, left-to-right tie-breaking.

When would you choose the two-paths LCA over the single-traversal one?

The single traversal is O(n) time, O(h) space and the version interviewers expect, but it silently returns a wrong node when one of the keys is absent. The two-paths method also runs in O(n) and reports a missing key honestly, at the cost of two traversals and two O(h) path lists. For BSTs neither is needed: walk down comparing keys in O(h). For many LCA queries on a fixed tree, preprocess with binary lifting (O(n log n) build, O(log n) per query).

Why is counting a complete binary tree O(log² n) and not O(n)?

At any node of a complete tree the left or the right subtree is perfect, and a perfect subtree of height h has 2^h − 1 nodes without being visited. Measuring the left and right spine heights costs O(log n); only one child needs a recursive call, so there are O(log n) such calls — O(log n) × O(log n). The same completeness is why heaps fit in an array with children at 2i + 1 and 2i + 2.
